title: On the Price of Privacy for Language Identification and Generation
claim: Privacy costs little or nothing: the retained exponent saturates beyond a threshold, and achievability and impossibility bounds match up to constants.
layout: 2 side-by-side log-log plots; shaded gap band between achieved and impossible curves
description: Two side-by-side log-log line plots share the x-axis, privacy parameter epsilon, running from 1e-3 to 10. Panel (a), titled identification, plots the fraction of the non-private exponent kept for three horizons f=5, 20 and 100, shown in light, medium and dark blue. Each curve rises linearly on the log-log axes, then flattens at 1, and larger f reaches the plateau at smaller epsilon. Panel (b), titled generation (Example 5.5), uses orange. A solid line shows the exponent achieved by Thm 4.4 and a dashed line shows the impossibility bound from Thm 5.4. A light orange shaded band fills the gap between them. Both lines rise linearly with epsilon and then level off, so the band stays a constant factor wide. Legends sit inside the plots.
caption: The price of pure privacy, read off our theorems. (a) Identification: the fraction of the non-private exponent that Theorem 3.4(a) keeps is min{1, 2𝜀𝑓}, because the privacy exponent 𝜀𝑛/(4 𝑓) overtakes the sampling exponent 𝑛/(8 𝑓2) at 𝜀= 1/(2 𝑓). The horizon 𝑓(𝑛) grows with 𝑛, so privacy is free at every fixed 𝜀. (b) Generation on the pair of Example 5.5: Theorem 4.4(a) achieves the exponent min{1/64, 𝜀/32} per sample, and Theorem 5.4 rules out any exponent above −log(1 −𝜃𝜀/4). Both edges of the band grow linearly in 𝜀and then level off, so on this pair the factor Θ(min{1, 𝜀}) is sharp.
abstract: Large language models train on sensitive user data, so we ask what differential privacy (DP) costs in language learning. We study private language identification and generation in the agnostic statistical setting. For identification, privacy is free: at every fixed $\varepsilon$, pure DP and $(\varepsilon,Î´)$-DP with $Î´\ge n^{-O(1)}$ keep the non-private rate $\exp(-r(n))$ for every $r(n)=o(n)$. For generation, the price depends on what is public. With a public witness bound, pure DP loses at most a factor $Î(\min\{1,\varepsilon\})$ in the exponent, and on suitable two-language collections the optimal rate is $\exp(-Î(\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\,n))$. Without such a bound, pure DP can lose the exponential rate itself, already for two languages: every rate $\exp(-o(n))$ stays achievable, but no exponential rate is. On these collections, $(\varepsilon,Î´)$-DP keeps an exponential rate if and only if $\log(1/Î´)=o(n)$. Three facts about pure DP drive the proofs. It turns a robustness margin into an exponentially small error. It obeys a private form of Le Cam's two-point bound. And it cannot see the absence of a string.
